lines: Up to now, every engine we've looked at reads a table this chapter actually built, somewhere on this machine.
This one is different -- a platform running on infrastructure nobody here can touch directly.
Everything from here comes straight from that platform's own published documentation.
Think about any table you've worked with that got split into chunks for storage.
Did a person sit down and decide where those boundaries went, or did the system just figure it out on its own?
Guess before the next slide answers it.
answer: Nobody draws those boundaries by hand here.
The system decides them on its own, every time.

lines: Picture a block of storage somewhere between the size of a small photo album and a feature film, holding one slice of a table.
Nobody carves that block out ahead of time -- it just appears as data lands.
Thousands, sometimes millions of these sit underneath one ordinary-looking table.
Each one of those blocks carries a little note about what range of values lives inside it, per column.
A filter reads those notes first and throws out whole blocks without opening them.
That's the entire trick behind a query that somehow skips most of a giant table.
Now imagine those blocks start overlapping in value -- block one and block eight both holding some of the same range.
The more that happens, the less a filter can throw away in one pass.
A background process watches for exactly that, and quietly rewrites things before anyone has to ask.
Here's a different kind of question: finding one specific needle in a haystack of distinct values, not a whole range.
Does the same trick from a moment ago -- skipping blocks by range -- still get you there fast?
Or does that particular shape of question need something else entirely?
answer: A separate, purpose-built lookup mechanism takes over for that one.

lines: That separate mechanism builds its own lookup structure, sitting beside the block metadata, not instead of it.
It's tuned for exactly one shape of question: find this one value, or this one fragment of text, fast.
Range-shaped questions never needed it; pinpoint questions do.
Here's the payoff of never rewriting a block in place: an old version simply never disappears on its own.
For a while you can still ask the system to show you exactly how things looked before a change.
Past that window, a second, much stricter safety net still holds the data a little longer, reachable only by the platform's own support team.
Two more things fall out of that same never-rewritten guarantee, almost for free.
Making a full copy of a table costs nothing at the moment you make it, because both copies point at the exact same unchanged blocks underneath.
Handing a table to someone else works the same way -- nothing physically moves, because nothing underneath ever had to.
One rule, underneath every single thing shown here: a block never gets rewritten once it's written.
Skipping blocks by range, cleaning up overlap, holding old versions, copying for free, handing off without moving data -- all of it follows from that one rule.
A second platform, built on entirely different infrastructure, is next -- and this sandbox can't touch that one either.
